newsitem.title: USA: Tax cut bill prompts tug-of-war on tax increases.
newsitem.headline: Tax cut bill prompts tug-of-war on tax increases.

text.p: Politicians do not like to raise taxes, but when put on the spot while drafting tax cut legislation they chose to hit tobacco over airlines, and airlines over Indian tribal casinos.

The Senate Finance Committee after hours behind closed doors emerged late Thursday with the surprise proposal to raise taxes on cigarettes which ended up in its tax bill. With the money from the tobacco tax, the committee then reduced the amount of revenues needed from proposed airline taxes.

The House Ways and Means Committee a week earlier faced the choice of imposing a tax on Indian tribal gaming tables or increasing international arrival and departure fees. In that instance Indian tribes were spared, the airlines were not.

"The airlines were caught flat-footed by what the House did and marshalled their troops to emergency status as quickly as they could, but they've probably just come up to battle strength at this point," said Robert Reischauer, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.
"And now of course the cigarette folks who were probably at home sleeping have now gone into the command bunker and are marshaling their forces," he said.
"So somewhere out there there's some unsuspecting interest that is probably going to get it between the ears out of the blue in a week," Reischauer added.

The House and Senate were scheduled to vote on their respective tax bills during the coming week. At that point members of Congress who oppose various provisions will have their say and some may be given a shot at amending the bills.

The tax legislation aims to fulfil the budget agreement between congressional leaders and the White House that called for a $135 billion in tax cuts over five years. But it also called for $50 billion in revenue increases for a net $85 billion cut.
The real crescendo will come when House and Senate conferees sit down to settle all the tug-of-wars and polish a final bill.
That will take place against the backdrop of competing interests and White House pronouncements of what would and would not be acceptable.
House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, has repeatedly said there would be no point drafting a bill that the president would veto.
As it stands, the House bill would not increase cigarette taxes and during the Ways and Means Committee debate a proposal to raise the tobacco tax was voted down.

Representative Jim Bunning, a Kentucky Republican who led the charge in the House committee against the cigarette proposal, said he was "disappointed" at the Senate Finance Committee action. "It would be devastating to the small tobacco farmers I represent," he said.
The Senate bill would raise the federal cigarette tax by 20 cents per pack, which would be on top of the current 24-cent tax.
The House tax bill would raise more revenues from international arrival and departure fees than the Senate bill.
House Republican leaders would not venture a forecast on whether the cigarette tax increase would survive and be implanted in the final tax bill.
"I have no prejudgment at this time for it, or against it," said House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican.
"I'm not going to take a position on it," Archer said. "It's not in our House bill, we'll deal with it in conference."
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, sidestepped questions on how the cigarette tax increase would fare, calling the Senate tax bill "a good starting package."

The tobacco settlement announced Friday might actually help the industry fight a cigarette tax increase, Reischauer said. Tobbacco companies could argue that they had already agreed to spend large sums of money for social programmes and question "Why are you hitting us again?" Reischauer said.
